title: How do you handle a request that takes way longer than a normal API call?
summary: Why a synchronous HTTP call is the wrong shape for genuinely long work, and how the accept-and-poll (or webhook) pattern replaces it.

slides.sectionTitle: Snapshot: why "just raise the timeout" loses
slides.markdown:
This question checks whether you recognize a synchronous HTTP call as the wrong shape for genuinely long-running work. "Just raise the timeout" is a losing answer because it treats the symptom, not the cause — it still holds a connection open for the full duration and pushes the same problem onto every layer in between.

The strong answer names the async pattern that replaces the synchronous call entirely: accept immediately, do the work in the background, let the caller check back or get notified.

Ask: **how long does the work actually take**, and does the caller need the result immediately or can they be notified later? A call that takes 3 seconds is a different conversation than one that takes 90.

Also ask: is the caller a **browser, a mobile client, or a server** that can receive a callback? A server-to-server caller can receive a webhook; a browser tab that might close can't reliably wait for one, which changes which async pattern fits.

Don't hold the HTTP connection open for the full duration of the work. Instead: **accept the request, return immediately with a reference**, and let the caller check back on progress or be notified when it's done.

This single shift — from "wait for the answer" to "here's a receipt, come back later" — is the core of every correct answer to this question, whatever specific mechanism you use to implement it.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: 202 Accepted plus a job_id
slides.markdown:
A worked example — a video-transcoding endpoint returns immediately with a job reference:

```
POST /videos/transcode
-> 202 Accepted
   { "job_id": "job_9f2a", "status": "queued" }

GET /jobs/job_9f2a
-> { "status": "processing", "progress": 0.6 }
... later ...
-> { "status": "done", "result_url": "https://.../video.mp4" }
```

The client polls `GET /jobs/{job_id}` for status, or a **webhook fires** when it's done if the caller registered a callback URL up front — either way, no connection sits open for the 90 seconds of actual transcoding work.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a report endpoint that got slower
slides.markdown:
A concrete scenario: a report-generation endpoint that used to take 2 seconds now takes **90 seconds** for a large customer's data, because the underlying dataset grew. Keeping it synchronous means the client's HTTP library times out at its own 30-second default and **retries** — generating the same expensive report twice for a request that was actually still running fine, just slowly.

This is the trap: the client's timeout has nothing to do with whether the server request is healthy, so a slow-but-working request looks identical to a failed one from the client's side, and gets duplicated.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: why raising every timeout doesn't scale
slides.markdown:
![Timeout propagates backward through the stack](assets/timeout-propagation.svg)

Raising the client and server timeouts to "just wait longer" ties up a request-handling thread or connection for the full duration of the work. Worse, every layer in between — load balancer, API gateway, reverse proxy — needs its own timeout raised to match, or it cuts the request off first.

One slow endpoint's needs end up propagating onto the timeout configuration of the entire stack, which doesn't scale as more endpoints have different duration profiles.

assets.alt: Timeout propagates backward through the stack

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Async job patterns add real complexity a simple synchronous call didn't need: a **job store** to track status, a **status API** for polling, and **retry/idempotency** handling for job creation itself, so a client's retried "create job" request doesn't spin up the same expensive work twice.

This complexity is only worth it once "just wait" genuinely stops working — for a call that reliably completes in 200ms, adding a job store and polling endpoint is pure overhead. Name both sides: the pattern solves a real problem, but it isn't free.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the client polls every second for 90 seconds
slides.markdown:
Expect: **"the client polls every second for 90 seconds — is that OK?"** Usually not at scale — 90 status checks per job, multiplied across every concurrent job, adds meaningful load to the status endpoint for information that mostly hasn't changed between checks.

Recommend **polling backoff** (check less frequently as elapsed time grows), or better, a **webhook or WebSocket push** so the server notifies the client the moment status actually changes, instead of the client guessing when to ask.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the job fails halfway through
slides.markdown:
Expect: **"the job fails halfway through — what does the status endpoint return, and can the client retry just the failed part?"** A **status enum that distinguishes retryable failure from terminal failure** — a transient timeout calling a downstream service is retryable, a malformed input is terminal and retrying won't help.

If the work is resumable, store enough **job state to restart from a checkpoint** rather than from scratch — for a multi-step transcode, that might mean recording which step last completed successfully, so a retry skips the steps already done.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: raising every timeout up the stack
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "This call is timing out — let's just raise the timeout at every layer until it stops."

**Why it's wrong:** it accommodates one slow operation by making every layer in the stack tolerate long waits, tying up threads and connections for the full duration and masking the real fix — moving that operation off the synchronous request path entirely.

**Correct model:** treat a repeatedly-timing-out synchronous call as a signal to redesign it as async (accept-and-poll or webhook), not as a signal to keep raising timeouts until the symptom disappears.

Don't hold the connection open for long work — accept immediately with a job reference, then let the client poll a status endpoint or receive a webhook. Distinguish retryable from terminal failures, and checkpoint resumable work. The cost is a job store, a status API, and idempotent job creation — worth it once synchronous genuinely stops working.

For the request/response mechanics of this pattern, see [Long-Running and Async APIs](long-running-and-async-apis).
